lesson.title: The Half Power Point: Reading Magnitude Response in Decibels
lesson.summary: Magnitude response converts a filter's amplitude ratio into decibels, turning the famous 3 dB corner frequency point into an exact, verifiable number rather than a rule of thumb.
lesson.body:
Frequency Response covers the full behavior of |H(jw)|, and Decibel gives a logarithmic way to express ratios, defined for a voltage or amplitude ratio as dB = 20 log10(|H|). Magnitude Response is the marriage of these two ideas: instead of reporting |H(jw)| as a plain ratio between 0 and 1, it is reported in decibels, which compresses a huge dynamic range into manageable numbers and matches how human hearing and most measurement equipment perceive signal strength. A ratio of 1, meaning no attenuation at all, corresponds to 0 dB, since log10(1) equals 0, which is why an unfiltered passband always shows up as a flat line sitting right at the 0 dB reference.

Continue with the same RC low pass filter, R = 1000 ohms, C = 1 microfarad, corner frequency wc = 1000 rad/s, using the same three frequencies examined for phase response. At w = 100 rad/s, |H| = 0.99504, so the magnitude in decibels is 20 log10(0.99504) = 20 times (-0.002161) = -0.0432 dB, indistinguishable from 0 dB, meaning the passband is essentially flat there.

At w = 1000 rad/s, the corner frequency, |H| = 0.70711, so the magnitude in decibels is 20 log10(0.70711) = 20 times (-0.15051) = -3.0103 dB. This is the origin of the famous 3 dB point that shows up throughout filter design, the frequency at which output power has dropped to half its low frequency value, since power is proportional to voltage squared and a 3 dB drop in voltage magnitude corresponds to a factor of 2 drop in power, because 10 log10(0.5) equals -3.0103 as well. The two definitions of the 3 dB point, half power and 0.7071 magnitude ratio, are the same statement in two different units.

At w = 10000 rad/s, one decade above the corner, |H| = 0.09950, so the magnitude in decibels is 20 log10(0.09950) = 20 times (-1.00216) = -20.043 dB. Compare the three results in sequence: -0.043 dB in the passband, -3.010 dB at the corner, -20.043 dB one decade above the corner. The jump from roughly 0 dB down to roughly -20 dB across that one decade is the signature of a first order filter's roll off rate, and it is exactly this pattern, expressed as a roll off measured in dB per decade, that gives the Bode Magnitude Plot its characteristic straight line shape once frequency is also plotted on a logarithmic axis.

Decibels are useful here for a very practical reason beyond compressing large ranges: when circuits are cascaded, stage after stage of filtering or amplification, their magnitude responses in decibels simply add, while their plain ratio magnitudes would have to be multiplied. That additive property is one of the main reasons magnitude response is almost always reported in decibels rather than as a raw fraction between 0 and 1. It also means a designer can predict the combined effect of two filters in series just by adding two numbers at each frequency, rather than multiplying two decimals, a small convenience that becomes a large one once several stages are involved.
